meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He who is not satisfied with a little is satisfied with nothing'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Epicurean in substance — it is Vatican Saying 68 — yet this exact English wording appears in no standard translation. A faithful paraphrase, not a verified quote.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 341–270 BC · Greek philosopher, founder of Epicureanism
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Epicurus’s — it is Vatican Saying 68 (Greek: Ouδέν ἱκανὸν ᾓ ὀλίγον τὸ ἱκανόν), which every standard translation renders as “Nothing is enough to one for whom enough is little.” But this exact English one-liner is a re-worded paraphrase that appears in no standard scholarly translation, and its origin as a rendering cannot be pinned to a confirmed source — so Epicurus is credited, but the precise wording is not verified.

source.heading: The saying behind the paraphrase

docMeta.dd: “Nothing is enough to one for whom enough is little.”

source.excerpt: Nothing is enough to one for whom enough is little.
trail: Standard translations of Vatican Saying 68 read “Nothing is enough to one for whom enough is little” (Greek Ouδέν ἱκανὸν ᾓ ὀλίγον τὸ ἱκανόν) — not the popular one-liner.
Wikiquote lists the popular wording and cites it to Eugene O’Connor’s The Essential Epicurus (1993), p. 99, but the exact wording could not be confirmed against that text.
A close reader of Epicurus searched “tirelessly” and could not find any source for this exact sentence, noting only that it echoes Epicurean teaching.
source.excerptNote: This is the standard scholarly rendering of Vatican Saying 68 (e.g. Peter Saint-Andre; N. H. Bartman). The popular English form — “He who is not satisfied with a little is satisfied with nothing” — says the same thing but flips it into a positive conditional, and matches none of these translations.
source.rightsNote: The ancient Greek of Vatican Saying 68 is public domain, but rights attach to the specific English wording displayed here. That wording matches no translation we could identify: it is not the pre-1931 Bailey rendering, nor Saint-Andre, nor a confirmed O’Connor line. As an anonymous modern paraphrase with no verified translator and no evidence of pre-1931 publication, its copyright status cannot be asserted, so we mark it uncertain rather than claim public domain.

author.name: Epicurus
author.heading: About Epicurus
author.metaLine: 341–270 BC · Greek philosopher, founder of Epicureanism
author.bio: Epicurus (341–270 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher who founded Epicureanism and taught in his Athenian “Garden.” He held that pleasure — understood as tranquility (ataraxia) and freedom from bodily pain — is the highest good, best reached by limiting desire to what is natural and necessary. Almost none of his voluminous writing survives; we have a few letters and two collections of maxims, the Principal Doctrines and the Vatican Sayings.

misattribution.heading: Misquote, not misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong author — the idea really is Epicurus’s. It is a case of the wrong words: a smooth modern paraphrase standing in for a saying that scholars translate quite differently.

items.why: Every standard translation of Vatican Saying 68 keeps the Greek structure — “Nothing is enough to one for whom enough is little” (Saint-Andre, Bartman, and the Society of Epicurus study guide all agree). The famous one-liner recasts it as a positive conditional found in none of them.
Wikiquote pins the exact wording to Eugene O’Connor’s The Essential Epicurus (1993), but the wording could not be confirmed in that text, and a specialist reader could find no source at all.

misattribution.truthLine: The substance is authentically Epicurean — it is Vatican Saying 68 — even though this exact English sentence is a modern rephrasing rather than a verified translation.

context.heading: Why it fits Epicurus
lead: For Epicurus, the route to a happy life was not acquiring more but wanting less. Desires that are neither natural nor necessary — for wealth, status, luxury — are boundless by nature, so chasing them guarantees permanent dissatisfaction. Vatican Saying 68 makes the point sharply: to a person who treats ‘enough’ as too little, no amount will ever be enough.

That is exactly what the popular one-liner captures. Whoever first rephrased it into “He who is not satisfied with a little is satisfied with nothing” distilled a real Epicurean idea — which is why the attribution to Epicurus is fair even though the words are not his.
detailsBody: The Vatican Sayings are a collection of 81 short Epicurean maxims preserved in a 14th-century Greek manuscript in the Vatican Library and first published in 1888. Some are by Epicurus himself and some by his followers; VS 68 is generally treated as Epicurus’s own.
context.pull: To one who treats ‘enough’ as too little, nothing will ever be enough.
